products.overview: Visible light and NIR-I imaging both hit the same wall: biological tissue scatters and absorbs at those wavelengths, and autofluorescence buries whatever signal makes it through. Push into the short-wave infrared — 700 to 1600 nm — and that wall mostly disappears. Tissue becomes transparent enough to image structures conventional systems simply cannot reach.
features: Ultra-Low-Noise Alizé™ 1.7 Camera: Deep-cooled InGaAs sensor at -60°C, the foundation of the system's sensitivity.
Full NIR-II Spectral Coverage: 700–1600 nm, exploiting the window where tissue is most transparent.
Zero Background Autofluorescence: Removes the noise floor that limits contrast on visible and NIR-I systems.
High-Intensity Multi-Wavelength Laser Illumination: 670, 760, 808, and 890 nm, with adjustable power density per application.
2 cm Imaging Depth: Signal-to-noise sufficient to resolve structures conventional systems can't reach.
Up to 10 Emission Channels: Simultaneous multiplexed tracking of distinct fluorescent labels.
Three Imaging Modes: Fluorescence, reflectance, and overlay, in one platform.
Variable Field of View: 80×64 mm for a full mouse, down to 50×40 mm for a single organ.
Motorized Z, Manual XY Stage: Precise, repeatable sample positioning.
50mm f/1.4 Lens: Standard optics matched to the system's imaging requirements.

comparison.disclaimer: The comparison isn't close on depth or contrast — it's the reason NIR-II imaging exists as a category. Where a study's targets sit near the surface and scattering isn't a limiting factor, a NIR-I system remains adequate. Where the structure of interest is buried under bone, tissue, or pigment, that's precisely the gap IR VIVO™ was built to close.

faqs.question: What is IR VIVO™ used for?
faqs.answer: It's a preclinical in vivo imaging system operating in the NIR-II (SWIR) spectrum, used for fluorescence-guided surgery research, vascular and lymphatic tracking, biodistribution studies, brain imaging, and multiplexed biomarker visualization in small animals.

faqs.question: What wavelength range does it operate in?
faqs.answer: 700 to 1600 nm, the NIR-II or short-wave infrared spectrum, where biological tissue becomes highly transparent to light.

faqs.question: How deep can IR VIVO™ image?
faqs.answer: Signal-to-noise sufficient for imaging is achievable to depths of 2 cm.

faqs.question: Why does NIR-II imaging see through bone and pigmented tissue?
faqs.answer: Light scattering is dramatically minimized and background autofluorescence is completely eliminated at these wavelengths, which is what allows structures like the brain through intact bone or melanoma through skin to be resolved.

faqs.question: What camera does IR VIVO™ use?
faqs.answer: An ultra-low-noise Alizé™ 1.7 InGaAs camera, deep-cooled to -60°C. Some of Photon etc.'s materials also reference a ZephIR™ 1.7 camera option — confirm the exact configuration at specification stage.

faqs.question: How many fluorescent signals can be tracked at once?
faqs.answer: Up to 10 emission channels, allowing distinct anatomical and molecular signals to be tracked simultaneously in the same animal.

faqs.question: What illumination does the system use?
faqs.answer: Laser illumination at 670, 760, 808, and 890 nm, with adjustable power density.

faqs.question: What field of view does IR VIVO™ offer?
faqs.answer: A variable field of view from 80×64 mm, suited to a full mouse, down to 50×40 mm for an individual organ.

faqs.question: Can it monitor physiological signals without touching the animal?
faqs.answer: Yes. The fast frame rates of the InGaAs camera support contact-free cardiography and respiratory rate measurement in anesthetized or awake animals, without restraint.

faqs.question: What software controls the system?
faqs.answer: PHySpec, Photon etc.'s control software platform spanning their instrument range — confirm the specific feature scope for IR VIVO™ at configuration.

faqs.question: How much bench space does the system need?
Is there published research using IR VIVO™?
faqs.answer: Yes. Photon etc. references multiple peer-reviewed and preprint publications spanning NIR-II fluorophore development, nanoparticle imaging, tumor delineation, and vascular/lymphatic multiplexing.

longForm.heroHook: See the brain through intact bone. See melanoma through skin. Without opening either.
longForm.heroLead: Visible light and NIR-I imaging both hit the same wall: biological tissue scatters and absorbs at those wavelengths, and autofluorescence buries whatever signal makes it through. Push into the short-wave infrared — 700 to 1600 nm — and that wall mostly disappears. Tissue becomes transparent enough to image structures conventional systems simply cannot reach. IR VIVO™ is built entirely around that window. Photon etc.'s ultra-low-noise Alizé™ 1.7 InGaAs camera, deep-cooled to -60°C, paired with high-intensity laser illumination, delivers signal-to-noise clean enough to resolve features 2 cm deep — the mouse brain through intact skull, black melanoma through pigmented skin, vasculature no surface camera will ever show you. Up to 10 emission channels let distinct fluorescent labels be tracked simultaneously in the same animal, isolated by emission bandwidth across the NIR-II window. For oncology, neuroscience, and drug discovery teams who've hit the resolution ceiling of NIR-I systems, this is the platform built for what comes after it.

sections.title: Why the NIR-II Window Matters
body: Every photon travelling through tissue at visible or NIR-I wavelengths scatters repeatedly before it reaches a camera, and every scatter blurs the image and shortens the useful imaging depth.
Tissue itself fluoresces at those wavelengths — a background signal with nowhere to hide, sitting directly under whatever probe signal is being measured.

IR VIVO™ operates where both problems largely disappear: across 700–1600 nm, biological tissue becomes highly transparent, scattering drops dramatically, and background autofluorescence is completely eliminated rather than merely reduced.

That is the entire reason the system can resolve structures like the mouse brain through intact bone, or black melanoma through pigmented skin — targets that are, in practical terms, invisible to instruments working at shorter wavelengths, however sensitive those instruments are.

Set against what deep in vivo imaging needs: signal that survives passage through tissue is delivered by SWIR wavelengths where tissue is highly transparent; no background noise competing with the probe is delivered by autofluorescence being completely eliminated; depth conventional systems cannot reach is delivered by signal-to-noise sufficient to 2 cm; and structures hidden from visible/NIR-I imaging are demonstrated on brain-through-bone and melanoma imaging.
sections.disclaimer: Share the tissue depth and structure the study needs to resolve, and expected performance gets discussed against IR VIVO™'s demonstrated depth capability.

sections.title: Multiplexed Imaging in One Animal
sections.description: Running separate cohorts to track separate biomarkers costs animals, time, and introduces variability between groups that a single-animal comparison would avoid entirely. IR VIVO™'s up to 10 emission channels isolate distinct emission bandwidths across the NIR-II window, so multiple fluorescent labels can be tracked simultaneously in the same living animal. Published work using the platform has demonstrated exactly this — lymphatic and vascular signals imaged together in the same mouse, distinguished by their different emission bandwidths within the NIR-II region. That's not two separate images overlaid afterwards; it's genuinely simultaneous acquisition across isolated channels, which is what makes real-time correlation between anatomical and molecular signals possible rather than inferred.
